text: Two new copper chisels just came from the coppersmiths. Before my stonecutters use them, I need to know which one is longer. Build them both, then show me.
No headset today? Then come to my drafting table. Build both chisels here, then write me a full report on what you found.
Before the headset goes on, study your models. Learn each gray word. You will type it in the search box in VR.
Put on your headset. Click Explore, type Giza, and pick Pyramids of Giza. Then click Begin Solo.
Remember, a Flat is one tenth, a Rod is one hundredth, and a Unit is one thousandth. Build Chisel A on the left, then Chisel B.
Now write it with Number models. Chisel A, the sign, then Chisel B. A small cube is your decimal point.
Still have time? Build a third chisel and line all three up, shortest to longest. This part is just for you.
Step back so both chisels and your answer fit. Take a photo, or a short video. Then send it to Canvas.
Press the Meta button and click Quit. Then open Canvas and make sure your work is there.
Welcome back, builder. Yesterday we staked the base. Today we lay the first layer of stones.
A photographer took this picture about 150 years ago. See the rows of stone on my pyramid? Each row is one layer.
Now look at the giant blocks in front. Tap the glowing ring.
Back on my build site, every block in the first layer must be the same height. If one is off, the next layer will tilt.
My scribe measured one block: 1.486 meters. Look at the 8. What do you think it is worth?
Every digit has a value. Let’s find out what each one is worth.
The first layer is level.
Every digit in its place. Good work, builder.
Tomorrow we compare the blocks.
Day three, builder. The first layer is down. Now we need many more blocks for the next layers.
Most blocks are cut right here at Giza. The fine white stone comes by boat across the river. Tap the glowing ring.
See the rows of stone tombs? They belong to the king’s officials. Tap the glowing ring.
Every new block gets checked. Too tall, and the layer bumps. Too short, and it sags.
Two blocks just arrived: 1.49 meters and 1.487 meters. Which is taller?
More digits does not always mean more. Let’s check them the builder’s way.
The blocks are in order.
Every block checked, place by place. Good work, builder.
Tomorrow we round our measurements.
Day four, builder. Look at this map of Giza. A map maker drew it about one hundred seventy years ago.
From above, a pyramid is a perfect square. Tap the glowing ring.
Today my crews cut the stones for the passages inside the pyramid.
My scribes measure to the millimeter. But my stonecutters only need the nearest centimeter.
This stone measures 2.346 meters. To the nearest centimeter, what should the work order say?
Close enough is a skill. Let’s learn to round.
The passage stones are cut.
Every work order rounded just right. Good work, builder.
Tomorrow my inspectors check our work.
Hello! I am Hemiunu. About 4,500 years ago, King Khufu put me in charge of building his pyramid.
An artist drew it in the 1830s, more than 4,000 years after my crews finished. Every block you see, my crews set in place.
Look at the tip of the pyramid next door. Tap the glowing ring.
Now come back with me to the very first day. Nothing is built yet. First we mark the base: a perfect square.
My surveyors measure with rods. Tap the rod.
You came from the future with a meter stick. In 1925, a surveyor measured my north side with one. It came out 230 meters and a little more.
How exactly did he measure? After the decimal point, how many digits do you think we will need?
Let’s zoom into that last meter and find out.
The base is measured to the millimeter.
Good work, builder.
Tomorrow we need even more care.
